questions.stem: (a) What is a primary source? (b) Give ONE example of a primary source a historian could use to study the First World War.
markscheme: B1: evidence created during the period being studied, by someone who was there
B1: any valid example, e.g. a soldier's letter or diary from the trenches / a wartime photograph / a propaganda poster
questions.modelAnswer: (a) A primary source is evidence created during the period being studied, by people who were there — documents, objects, images or oral accounts. (b) For the First World War, examples include a soldier's letter home from the trenches, a trench diary, a wartime photograph or a government propaganda poster.

questions.stem: (a) What was the policy of appeasement? (b) Name the conference of September 1938 at which Britain agreed that Hitler could take the Sudetenland.
markscheme: B1: giving in to (some of) Hitler's demands in the hope of avoiding war
B1: the Munich Conference
questions.modelAnswer: (a) Appeasement was the British and French policy of giving in to some of Hitler's demands in the hope of avoiding another war. (b) The Munich Conference of September 1938, at which Chamberlain accepted the German takeover of the Sudetenland and returned home promising 'peace for our time'. When Hitler seized the rest of Czechoslovakia in March 1939, the policy was proved to have failed.

questions.stem: (a) Who unified China in 221 BCE and took the title of First Emperor? (b) What is the name of the vast collection of clay soldiers buried near Xi'an to guard his tomb?
markscheme: B1: Qin Shi Huang (accept: the king of Qin)
B1: the Terracotta Army
questions.modelAnswer: (a) Qin Shi Huang, the king of the state of Qin, defeated his rival states and proclaimed himself First Emperor of a unified China in 221 BCE. (b) The Terracotta Army — more than 8,000 life-sized clay soldiers, horses and chariots, each with individually modelled features, buried to protect him in the afterlife and rediscovered by farmers digging a well in 1974.

questions.stem: Explain how the Black Death (1347–1351) changed the position of peasants in England.
markscheme: B1: the plague killed between a third and a half of the population, creating a severe shortage of workers
B1: with labour scarce, surviving peasants could demand higher wages and refuse feudal duties
B1: attempts to hold peasants down (the Statute of Labourers, 1351) failed in the long run, and serfdom slowly faded away
questions.modelAnswer: The Black Death killed between a third and a half of England's population, so labour suddenly became scarce. Surviving peasants found lords competing for their work and could demand higher wages, move for better terms and refuse old feudal duties. The government tried to hold them down with the Statute of Labourers in 1351, which froze wages at pre-plague levels, but in the long run it failed: landlords increasingly replaced labour services with cash rents, and serfdom faded away over the following century.

questions.stem: Source A: an extract from the (fictional) diary of Hans Berger, a factory worker in Essen, written in 1936. "Three years ago I had no work and no hope — I queued at the soup kitchen like a beggar. Now I have a job building the new motorway, and last summer the Strength Through Joy scheme sent my whole family to the seaside for a week. My son loves the Hitler Youth and never stops talking about the camping. Not everyone dares to speak their mind these days, but for my family, at least, life is better." What can you infer from Source A about why many ordinary Germans supported the Nazi regime? Make THREE supported points, using a quotation for each.
markscheme: B1: the fall in unemployment won support, e.g. "I have a job building the new motorway" (accept "no work and no hope")
B1: state leisure schemes bought goodwill, e.g. "sent my whole family to the seaside"
B1: the youth movements attracted the young, e.g. "My son loves the Hitler Youth" (accept the hint of fear: "Not everyone dares to speak their mind")
questions.modelAnswer: The diary suggests several reasons why ordinary Germans supported the regime. First, the Nazis had ended the despair of unemployment: Berger once had "no work and no hope" but now says "I have a job building the new motorway". Second, state schemes improved daily life and bought goodwill — the Strength Through Joy programme "sent my whole family to the seaside". Third, the young were won over by the youth movements: "My son loves the Hitler Youth". Yet the diary also hints at the darker side of support: "Not everyone dares to speak their mind" suggests fear of the Gestapo helped keep criticism quiet.

questions.stem: State TWO mistakes made by the Provisional Government in 1917 that drove the Russian people towards the Bolsheviks.
markscheme: B1: it continued the unpopular First World War
B1: it kept postponing land reform (leaving the peasants' demands unanswered)
questions.modelAnswer: First, the Provisional Government chose to continue the war, so the casualties and food shortages went on. Second, it kept postponing land reform, disappointing the peasants who wanted the nobles' estates. These failures made Lenin's slogans — 'Peace, Land and Bread' and 'All Power to the Soviets' — speak directly to people's needs, and support drained away from the government towards the Bolsheviks.

questions.stem: "It was the atomic bombs, more than anything else, that forced Japan to surrender in August 1945." How far do you agree with this statement? Use your knowledge to support your judgement.
markscheme: B1: evidence for the bombs' decisiveness, e.g. Hiroshima (6 August) and Nagasaki (9 August) destroyed two cities after Japan ignored the Potsdam ultimatum

B1: evidence for other factors, e.g. the Soviet Union declared war and invaded Manchuria on 8 August, destroying Japan's hope of negotiating through Moscow (accept: Japan was already blockaded, bombed and starving)
B1: a supported judgement, e.g. the combination of the bombs and Soviet entry forced the decision, with Emperor Hirohito's intervention breaking the deadlock
questions.modelAnswer: There is a strong case for the bombs: Japan had ignored the Potsdam demand for unconditional surrender, and the destruction of Hiroshima on 6 August and Nagasaki on 9 August, killing well over 100,000 people, shocked its leaders. But other factors mattered too: on 8 August the Soviet Union declared war and invaded Manchuria, destroying Japan's last hope of negotiating peace through Moscow, and Japan was already defeated at sea, its cities firebombed and its people close to starvation. On balance I partly agree: the bombs delivered the immediate shock, but it was the combination of the bombings and the Soviet entry that forced the decision — and even then it took Emperor Hirohito's personal intervention to break the deadlock and announce surrender on 15 August 1945.

questions.stem: Explain why the drawing of the Partition borders in 1947 led to such chaos and violence.
markscheme: B1: Cyril Radcliffe, who had never been to India, was given barely five weeks to draw the borders through Punjab and Bengal
B1: the boundary was announced only after independence (14–15 August 1947), so millions did not know which country they were in
B1: the result was mass panic and migration — around 10–15 million people crossed the borders — and communal violence that killed an estimated one to two million
questions.modelAnswer: The borders were drawn in absurd haste: Cyril Radcliffe, a British lawyer who had never visited India, was given barely five weeks to divide the mixed provinces of Punjab and Bengal. Worse, the boundary was announced only after independence on 14–15 August 1947, so millions of people did not know which country they were in. Panic followed: Muslims fled towards Pakistan and Hindus and Sikhs towards India — around 10–15 million people in one of the largest migrations in history — and terrible communal violence, especially in Punjab, killed an estimated one to two million. The joy of freedom was inseparable from the trauma of Partition.
